description:
Wheel Bug (Arilus cristatus) - nymph

8 June 2016
Greenbelt Corridor Ray Roberts/Lewisville Lake FM 428 Access Area, Aubrey Branch
Denton County, Texas

Wheel Bug is the largest assassin bug in North America. While there are four species to the genus Arilus, only the species Cristatus occurs in the United States. Cristatus means "crested" because of the cog-like half-wheel mature Wheel Bugs develop on their backs. According to BugGuide's entry for Wheel Bug, its range includes most of the eastern United States (and the province of Ontario, Canada), south to Florida thence west to California. Its range encompasses Mexico and Central America, where it is said to occur as far south as Guatemala. The series Featured Creatures at the University of Florida writes this short thumbnail sketch of Wheel Bug: "The wheel bug, Arilus cristatus (Linnaeus), is a moderately common, widely distributed, beneficial assassin bug that preys on pest insects. However, its bite can be more severe than a bee sting, and both nymphs and adults should be avoided or handled with caution. Adult: The wheel bug adult usually measures from 1 to 1.25 inches long. This assassin bug is a dark, robust, grotesque creature with long legs and antennae, a stout beak, large eyes on a slim head, and a prominent thoracic, semicircular crest that resembles a cogwheel or chicken's comb. This is the only insect species in the United States with such a crest. The number of teeth (tubercles) in the crest varies from eight to 12. Females are larger than males, with the abdominal margins being more widely exposed in the females. A very fine yellowish pubescence is present over most of the body, except the elytral membrane which is iridescent bronze. The overall color is dark brown. Variable amounts of tiny white patches or granules are scattered throughout the pubescence. Nymphs: Nymphs have been described in detail by Readio (1927). Smaller nymphs are bright red with black marks. The last instar nymphs are darker. Nymphs lack the "wheel" or crest. To determine if a nymph is Arilus, consult Fracker and Usinger (1949)." Because of its extensive North American range, Wheel Bug is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. The Greenbelt Corridor FM 428 Access Area is administered by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.

description: This thing is one of the most unusual bugs in all my adventures. This one is called the Wheel Bug. The buzz saw like protrusion on its back is the wheel. They are in the assassin bug and true bug grouping. They are primarily gray with some black and darker color. This thing has a massive and sharp proboscis  that is used to stab its prey to death. They are stealthy hunters and are just as their group name implies Deadly Assassins. They like to ambush their prey when they are least suspecting and in the blink of an eye the insects that these things hunt don't know what hit them. They are slow at first but are swift for the kill. Their proboscis is used to inject digestive enzymes that slowly liquefy their prey's body tissue and just like a straw it sucks up the    bug like a 7-11 slupree. Gross but true. This is by far one of my favorite bugs but the thing is you don't want to try to handle one of these because they can do a wallop of a bite. I have never attempted to handle one but I have heard stories but if you do get bit it isn't all that bad. They just hurt like the dickens. They are  pretty large bugs and very easy to recognize. That wheel is unmistakable. It is one of the weirdest structures I have seen on an insect.

I already have this on file but this is a better picture. My mother took this one when we were observing it. I didn't realize it at the time but the red parts that make the triangles, the area where the wings fold and the round shape to the insect's carapace and side look so much like the Star Trek Next Generation Communicator badge. It is so funny to see this. It is just kind of funny to me seeing this. Anyway I am making this ID just because I never knew just how vibrant the warning colors are on this thing. I mean it is a very beautiful blood red color with some black and yellow. This one is very interesting and I just never noticed the true patterning to this little guy. The name of this one slips me at the moment but it is pretty interesting. It is a very pretty bug but those patterns only mean to "stay away I am dangerous" Assassin Bugs are a pretty neat group of insects and one of my all time favorites. They are stealthy like trained Ninja Assassins and are very swift to. Their prey doesn't know what hit them until it is too late. They are one of the natural worlds most sophisticated killing machines. They are truly licensed to kill.

description: Here is my record of the assassin bug that many of us documented at Amistad. A second illustration points out key parts of the insect. Differentiating R. hamatus from R. guttatus is not always simple but the original literature (Blatchley 1926) includes a key which describes the differences. I've included a marked up copy of my image (2nd pic) to illustrate my understanding of those differences. Simply put, on biguttatus *half* of the hardened basal part of the forewing (corium) is ALL yellow with no dark sliver splitting towards its base. This example from Louisiana shows a classic Rasahus biguttatus: https://bugguide.net/node/view/839960/bgimage In classic hamatus (as illustrated in a line drawing in Blatchley's original work), a substantial dark area penetrates towards the base of the corium on each wing, splitting the yellow and creating an "M"-shaped yellow patch on the basal part of the wings as shown in the present example. Often, the outer edge of that yellow M is also missing so that there is only yellow along the inner seams of the corium. The color on the narrow clavus, the sliver of the wing basal to the V-shaped seams on the corium, is variable but basically it is about 1/2 yellow on hamatus and 2/3 to 3/4 yellow on biguttatus (thus "in great part yellow" in Blatchley's original phrasing). The last element is the "connexivum" or the edge of the abdomen exposed on each side of the FWs. This is reportly widely visible AND boldly marked black and yellow on BOTH sexes of biguttatus. It is usually mostly pale on both sexes of hamatus and either wide (female) or narrow (male). As I understand it, the present bug shows all the correct marks for a male Rasahus hamatus.

description:
Favorite Meal
This is the adult version of the assassin bug.  Both it and the nymph form are fierce predators.  I keep finding them on my milkweed and with the adults, they seem to prefer flies for dinner.  Which is fine by me.
This time the bug was much more cooperative and I got several decent shots, although the bright sun was a bit too much.  I think it was too busy eating to pay much attention to me.
Assassin bugs have glands in their legs that produce a sticky glue-like substance.  They smear this over the hairs on their feet and legs and this creates a sticky layer that the prey cannot escape once grabbed.  
When the assassin bug nymphs hatch, they do not have the ability to produce the glue-like substance but the parent has taken care of that problem.  Mom has covered the egg cluster in sticky glue and the baby nymph wipe their legs along the egg cluster to gather some glue.

description:
Assassin Bug And Prey
The assassin bug is a good bug to have in your garden.  It won't hurt your plants and it eats the pest bugs that do hurt your plants.  Once they capture their prey, they use a hollow tube called a rostrum to pierce their prey and inject a digestive enzyme which quickly kills.  This lets them eat prey much larger than themselves.  I was fortunate enough to see this one eating a fly on my milkweed and it stayed there long enough for me to capture the image. Do not pick them up, they will cause a small wound that burns a little.  Won't kill you like it does prey but will hurt.
ID confirmed in bugguide here:  https://bugguide.net/node/view/1092213

description: The assassin bug (Pselliopus ssp), sometimes referred to as the "kissing bug" are a group of carnivorous, predatory, Insects that are common all along the Southern Hemisphere in areas that can support a lot of foliage, I.E. their hunting grounds. The particular assassin bug seen in the photo was prowling around the gardens in our backyard, and it wasn't the only one. While observing these small hunters, I had noticed that they move very carefully, always with their abdomen raised. The position of the front legs are always taken by the one behind it, very similar to a centipede or a cat. The assassin bug is a ambush predator, lying in wait till an opportunity to stake is present. When it captures its prey, usually another insect of similar size, it will immobilize the victim with front legs. Once the prey is caught, the assassin bug will uncurl the appendage under its head and stab it repeatedly with the sharp paint of the appendage, both killing and partially ingesting the prey. Assassin bugs are often referred to as a gardeners best friend because of their proficiency at disposing of insects that would otherwise eat the gardener's plants.

description:
Rowlett Creek Nature Preserve
This is another new bug that I found at the nature preserve.  The milkweed assassin bug gets its name because it looks like the milkweed bug.  Most insects that feed on milkweed are bright orange & black to tell predators that they are toxic due to eating the toxic milkweed plant juices.  The milkweed assassin bug is not toxic and does not eat milkweed, it is a predator that eats whatever insects it can catch, wherever it can catch them. It is a beneficial insect with it's preference for prey that are considered pests to farmers and gardeners. And it fools predators into thinking it is toxic with the orange & black.

More Drama On My Milkweed
When I checked my milkweed I found more life & death drama going on.  An assassin bug nymph has caught a tiny fly for its meal.  The experts tell me the prey is most likely a dark-winged fungus gnat.  That hollow tube of the nymph is sucking all the juices out of the fly. 
Photo 2:
It's A Jungle Out There!
There is always something like this going on with my milkweed plants.  Assassin bugs, spiders, wasps, preying mantis, anoles.  Lots of predators.  Which is why I bring inside any monarch caterpillars I find and why the statistics say only 5% of monarch eggs on milkweed make it to the butterfly stage.     
ID confirmed on bugguide here:  https://bugguide.net/node/view/1615726

description:
"The wheel bug (Arilus cristatus) is a species of large assassin bug in the assassin and kissing bug family Reduviidae (literally, "hangnail").

Behavior

Wheel bugs initiate predation by gripping and pinning their prey with their front legs.[9] The bug plunges its beak into its victim before injecting it with enzymes, paralyzing it and dissolving its insides, and proceeds to drain the resulting fluids.

The wheel bug is also noted to be very vicious in the wild, and cannibalistic behaviors between them have been noted; for example, nymphs may prey on one another and the female may feed on the male after mating is concluded.

Ecological significance

Wheel bugs are highly regarded by organic gardeners because they consume a variety of insects and their presence indicates a healthy, pesticide-free ecosystem. "They're the lion or the eagle of your food web," Dr. Michael J. Raupp, an entomologist at the University of Maryland, notes. "They sit on top. When you have these big, ferocious predators in your landscape, that tells me that this is a very healthy landscape, because all these other levels in your food web are intact."[10]

Though wheel bugs are a welcome agent of pest control, they also prey on several ecologically beneficial species, such as lady beetles and honey bees."

Visual Description: The size of this organism is fairly small, about the size of a quarter, including its leg length. This bug was located on a grill within a park that is also available for use by the public. This same grill was home to other insects such as spiders as well. This bug is mainly black with splotches of a red/orange color on its body. This bug is most likely a protostome due to its appearance and the suggested ID was a wheel bug, commonly known to live in Florida. Wheel bugs appear to be black and orange while young, as the molt as they grow. At a full adult size, wheel bugs have a changed appearance to a dusty grey, white color, significantly different from young wheel bugs.

Habitat of Organism: This organism was found in a park, crawling on a public grill. This organism is mainly known to live in Florida, some spots of Texas, and has been seen in California. These bugs commonly feed on other insects, especially caterpillars, which were present throughout the area observed and in close proximity to this bug. Because of its food choice, these bugs are known to make home to forests, parks, and shrubbery areas. They are also seen more readily in summer and fall climates.

References: 
1. http://entnemdept.ufl.edu/creatures/trees/wheel_bug.htm
2. https://www.insectidentification.org/insect-description.asp?identification=Wheel-Bug

description: The wheel bug is a species of large assassin bug in the family Reduviidae. The species is one of the largest terrestrial true bugs in North America, reaching up to 1.5 inches in length in their adult stage. They are sexually dimorphic, in that males are somewhat smaller than the females. They come from the order Hemiptera and the family Reduviidae. They are camouflaged and very shy, residing in leafy areas and hiding whenever possible. Specifically, habitats of the wheel bug include sunflowers, goldenrod, cotton, trunks of locust trees, and various fruit and tree groves. They have membranous wings, allowing for clumsy, noisy flight which can easily be mistaken for the flight of a large grasshopper. The adult is gray to brownish gray in color and black shortly after molting, but the nymphs (which do not yet have the wheel-shaped structure) have bright red or orange abdomens. This bug was found in a small tree hiding under the leaves. This small tree was near a pond at Reedy Creek park. The type of plant was not identified.

description:
I found this type of bug crawling around my house. It looks almost like a spider but it is clearly not. This bug has six legs with two "antennae"(not sure if that's what you call it) in the front. The bug's abdomen is a bright red with a few speckles of black. The bug's head and thorax is black, though where the head connects to the rest of the body, it is white. On the tips of the "antennae", are brown. The bug's size is around the size of my thumb and moves pretty fast. 

I did ask someone from the company, Team Pest, about what genus species this bug identified as and they said that it was a Wheel bug; a type of assassin bug. They come from the family Reduviidae. They are one of the largest terrestrial true bugs around. Their scientific name is Arilus cristatus and they are sexually dimorphic; meaning that  the two sexes of this bug exhibit different characteristics beyond sexual organs. They are beneficial bugs, which means they provide services helpful to other species, such as: pollination and pest control. You should be wary of handling them as they can give some nasty bites; however, they do not come off as aggressive as they try to avoid contact. After looking at some pictures of wheel bugs, I can say that I agree with this identification.

description:
Wheel Bug (Arilus cristatus)

6 July 2020
Clear Creek Natural Heritage Center (CCNHC)
Denton, Denton County, Texas

---
Wheel Bug is the largest assassin bug in North America. While there are four species to the genus Arilus, only the species Cristatus occurs in the United States. Cristatus means "crested" because of the cog-like half-wheel mature Wheel Bugs develop on their backs. According to BugGuide's entry for Wheel Bug, its range includes most of the eastern United States (and the province of Ontario, Canada), south to Florida thence west to California. Its range encompasses Mexico and Central America, where it is said to occur as far south as Guatemala. The series Featured Creatures at the University of Florida writes this short thumbnail sketch of Wheel Bug: "The wheel bug, Arilus cristatus (Linnaeus), is a moderately common, widely distributed, beneficial assassin bug that preys on pest insects. However, its bite can be more severe than a bee sting, and both nymphs and adults should be avoided or handled with caution. Adult: The wheel bug adult usually measures from 1 to 1.25 inches long. This assassin bug is a dark, robust, grotesque creature with long legs and antennae, a stout beak, large eyes on a slim head, and a prominent thoracic, semicircular crest that resembles a cogwheel or chicken's comb. This is the only insect species in the United States with such a crest. The number of teeth (tubercles) in the crest varies from eight to 12. Females are larger than males, with the abdominal margins being more widely exposed in the females. A very fine yellowish pubescence is present over most of the body, except the elytral membrane which is iridescent bronze. The overall color is dark brown. Variable amounts of tiny white patches or granules are scattered throughout the pubescence. Nymphs: Nymphs have been described in detail by Readio (1927). Smaller nymphs are bright red with black marks. The last instar nymphs are darker. Nymphs lack the "wheel" or crest. To determine if a nymph is Arilus, consult Fracker and Usinger (1949)." Because of its extensive North American range, Wheel Bug is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. Clear Creek Natural Heritage Center (CCNHC) is administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

description: Order Hemiptera, the ringed assassin bug is a secondary consumer, eating small insects such as mosquitoes and other bugs. It can be identified by the distinctive white and black banded legs. It also has a dull or bright orange body with black markings on the side of it. It can be distinguished from similar looking insects by the wings and lack of abdominal spines. The ringed assassin bug has a three stage life cycle: egg, nymph, and adult. After hatching from an egg, it takes around two months for the nymph to transition into being an adult, and several molts. The individual I saw was an adult. I was not able to sex it. Assassin bugs live near forests, meadows, fields, and brush. Typically, these bugs are observed further south, but recently have been pushed north due to climate change. One competitor for the ringed assassin bug is the blue eyed darner butterfly, which also eats mosquitoes, and a predator is the house sparrow, who eats bugs.
